# Creative Conventions

These are the writer's standards, not craft law. Cite them as their own: *"this breaks your
scene-economy rule"*, never *"this breaks the rules of scene construction"*. A writer may
retire a convention at any time. Take that statement at face value. Stop applying the
convention for the session.

Attach evidence before citing a convention. Name the scene. Name the beat. State what makes it
a breach. A finding that only asserts the rule was broken is not a diagnosis.

## Which Modes May Cite This

| Mode | Use |
|---|---|
| **Diagnose** | Full. Treat a breach as any other finding. |
| **Adversarial** | Full. Lead with the worst breach when it is the weakest thing present. |
| **Copyedit** | Only the drift conventions, and only inside the passage being edited. |
| **Interrogate** | Ask a question a convention suggests. Never state the breach. |
| **Reflect** | Never. Do not add a convention check. |
| **Generate** | Never. |

`creative-compliance` still governs. A convention never licenses a fix. *"Scene 12 ends where
it started"* is a finding. *"Give her the letter earlier"* is a fix and belongs to the writer.

## Hard Conventions

These are execution failures. Flag every instance plainly.

### Overexplaining after the beat lands

The scene shows the thing, then a paragraph tells the reader what they just saw. Quote the line
that does the telling. Name the beat it repeats.

A character explaining something to another character who genuinely does not know it is not a
breach. The test is who the explanation is for.

### Telegraphing

The setup is so deliberate that it gives away the payoff before it arrives. Name the setup.
Name the payoff. State what gave it away.

Deliberate dramatic irony that the writer built on purpose is not a breach. The reader is meant
to know, and the tension comes from waiting. Ask which reading applies only in Interrogate. In
Diagnose, state which reading the text supports.

### POV slippage

Flag knowledge, perception, or interiority the viewpoint character cannot have. Quote the line.
State what the viewpoint character would have to do to know it.

An established omniscient or shifting POV is not a breach. Check the book's declared POV
structure before flagging. Find that structure in the per-book conventions below.

### Stakes resting on something met once

A threat, a bond, or a loss carries weight the text has not established. Name the stake. Name
the single appearance it rests on. State the distance between the stake and its appearance.

## Default Conventions

Scene economy governs by default. Exceptions exist, and deliberate breaks are choices, not
failures. Flag the break. State that it reads as unintended. State why. Stop there.

When the writer says it was deliberate, drop it for the session. Record that in `context/`.

### Enter late, exit early

A scene starts at the last possible moment and ends at the first. Name the beats before the real
start. Name the beats after the real end.

### Exit on the turn, not the settle

Apply this convention as a stricter version of the previous one. Cut when the thing changes,
not after the characters have absorbed it. The aftermath beat is the usual offender.

### Every scene changes something

By the end, someone knows, wants, or can do something they could not at the start. When nothing
shifts, say so: *"this scene ends where it started."* Name the state at both ends.

### No scene does work another scene already did

Two scenes carry the same beat. The second argument relitigates the first, or the second
revelation repeats a thing already revealed. Name both scenes. Name the beat they share.

### Because of, or in spite of — never and then

Every scene follows from an earlier one as a consequence or reaction against it. Find the earlier
scene that caused this one or that this one pushes back against. When you cannot find one, the
missing antecedent is the finding.

The finding is the missing antecedent, not the adjacency. Three cases are not breaches:

- The opening scene has nothing prior.
- A parallel plotline runs its causality to that thread's own last appearance, not to the
  scene physically before it.
- Two scenes placed together for contrast rather than consequence.

Search the whole preceding text for the antecedent before reporting one missing.

## Per-Book Conventions

The conventions above hold across everything the writer writes. A book's own rules — tense,
POV structure, chapter length, whether prologues are allowed — belong to that vault.

Read `_editor-notes/context/` for the book's rules, per `creative-vault`. When a book's rule
contradicts a convention here, the book wins. State in one line that you are following the
book's rule.

When a convention check needs a per-book rule that no context file records, state what you need.
Let the writer answer. Do not assume the default.
